title: In the Room
gist: A BCG executive-coaching column argues that AI is the first tech shift where being a late adopter is the risky choice rather than the safe one, and that enterprise AI is 70% people work, 20% data, and only 10% technology. The actionable prescription: pick two or three high-value problems, aim at 'aperture expansion' (work humans cannot do at all) rather than headcount cuts, accept a 70% success rate as a win, and keep first deployments away from safety- or compliance-critical processes. (The raw title 'In the Room' is the column's series name, not the subject; the text is about balancing AI urgency against risk.)

themes.theme: AI adoption timing breaks the cloud playbook

insights.claim: Unlike the cloud transition, where a company could be the 25th adopter and still be fine, AI offers no safe late-follower position, so delay is now the higher-risk posture for incumbents.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Supports a dispersion trade: in AI-exposed sectors, the gap between early enterprise adopters and laggards should widen faster than it did in the cloud cycle, so laggard multiples deserve a discount rather than a wait-and-see benefit of the doubt.
insights.quote: With earlier tech shifts, like moving to the cloud, you could afford to be the 25th company to adopt and still be fine. AI doesn’t work that way.
insights.locator: Your board is right to push.

insights.claim: Boards across C-suites are uniformly pushing management teams to move on AI, making board pressure — not management conviction — a primary driver of current enterprise AI spending decisions.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Board-driven mandates tend to produce budget that gets spent regardless of near-term ROI evidence — near-term supportive for AI vendors and services, but a signal to scrutinize whether announced programs are conviction-led or box-ticking.
insights.quote: My board is pushing on AI. I know we need to move. But my team isn’t ready, and I’m worried we’ll rush into decisions that backfire.
insights.locator: For BCG’s first In the Room column

insights.claim: The single most frequent question a BCG executive coach receives from CEOs right now is how to balance AI urgency against the risk of rushed decisions, indicating the bottleneck at the top of large enterprises is decision confidence rather than technology access.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Demand for AI change-management and advisory services should stay strong even if raw technology spend digests — the scarce input is executive decision support, not models.
insights.quote: I picked the question I get more often than any other right now.
insights.locator: For BCG’s first In the Room column

themes.theme: 70/20/10: AI transformation is a people problem

insights.claim: In an enterprise AI journey the effort splits roughly 10% technology, 20% data, and 70% people work, meaning the binding constraint on AI value capture is organizational, not model capability.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: If 90% of the work sits outside the model layer, value accrues disproportionately to data platforms, integrators and change-management providers rather than to model vendors alone — and explains why model capability gains don't translate one-for-one into enterprise productivity.
insights.quote: In any AI journey, technology is only 10% of the equation, and data is another 20%. But most of the work, 70%, is people work.
insights.locator: 1. Don’t think of the issue as a technology problem.

insights.claim: Employee statements that they 'aren't ready' for AI are usually fear about job security and the devaluation of hard-won expertise rather than genuine capability gaps, so treating it as a training problem misdiagnoses the resistance.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Adoption rates inside enterprises are a sentiment variable, not a licensing variable — watch seat utilization and workflow embedding, not seats sold, when underwriting enterprise AI software revenue durability.
insights.quote: When people on your team say they “aren’t ready,” don’t hear that only as resistance. Often, what lies beneath it is fear.
insights.locator: When people on your team say they

insights.claim: Leaders should explicitly tell staff that AI is meant to extend rather than replace their expertise, while simultaneously being honest that employees who learn to work with AI will out-compete those who don't.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Implies intra-firm labor stratification rather than mass displacement in the near term — a wage-dispersion story inside white-collar roles that affects labor-cost models more than headcount forecasts.
insights.quote: The goal is not to replace their expertise. The goal is to extend it.
insights.locator: Start by saying the true thing out loud.

insights.claim: Adoption should be driven by embedding AI in the flow of existing real work — preparing for customer conversations, summarizing complex inputs, drafting first-version recommendations, pressure-testing decisions, pattern-finding in feedback — rather than by standalone AI initiatives.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Favors AI delivered inside incumbent workflow suites and systems of record over standalone AI point tools, since the former sit where the work already happens.
insights.quote: The point is to help people experience AI as something they can use, not just something being done to them.
insights.locator: That means giving people practical, low-risk ways

themes.theme: Aperture expansion beats cost-cutting as the AI prize

insights.claim: Implementing AI in 50 places at once is the fastest route to failure and team burnout; enterprises should point AI at only two or three problems that matter most, such as customer churn if that is the biggest issue.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Companies announcing sprawling, company-wide AI rollouts are more likely to disappoint than those naming two or three concrete use cases — use use-case concentration as a quality screen on AI capex disclosures.
insights.quote: The quickest way to fail and burn out your team is to implement AI in 50 places at once.
insights.locator: 2. Don’t try to boil the ocean.

insights.claim: Making cost-cutting and headcount reduction the primary AI goal is the wrong objective; the larger prize is 'aperture expansion' — enabling work humans cannot do at all — with efficiency savings arriving as a byproduct.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Cuts against the dominant 'AI equals margin expansion via headcount' narrative — revenue-expansion AI stories may prove more durable than labor-substitution stories, and pure cost-out AI pitches deserve more skepticism.
insights.quote: And don’t make cost-cutting and headcount reduction the primary goal. ... That’s what I call aperture expansion.
insights.locator: And don’t make cost-cutting and headcount reduction

insights.claim: The concrete examples of AI-enabled work that was previously impossible are screening 100 million molecular combinations for a new drug or material, answering a customer's hardest question in 30 minutes instead of a week, and settling a home or auto claim in hours instead of weeks.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Names the three verticals where AI economics are framed as step-change rather than incremental — pharma/materials discovery, customer service latency, and claims settlement cycle time are the places to look for measurable operating-metric improvement.
insights.quote: screening 100 million molecular combinations to find a new drug or material, answering a customer's hardest question in 30 minutes instead of a week, or settling the claim on a wrecked home or car in hours instead of weeks
insights.locator: The real prize AI can deliver

insights.claim: Organizations tolerate roughly a 7% human error rate while demanding 100% accuracy from machines, an asymmetric standard that blocks AI deployment in processes where AI would already outperform people.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: This psychological hurdle, not model quality, is the gating factor on enterprise AI penetration rates — a shift in governance standards would unlock deployment faster than any model upgrade.
insights.quote: we tend to accept a 7% human error rate while demanding 100% perfection from machines
insights.locator: 3. Redefine what success looks like for your team.

insights.claim: Because AI is statistical rather than deterministic, management should set a 70% success rate as the definition of a win and treat the 30% failure rate as a learning input, with failed experiments killed quickly via blameless post mortems.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Sets an explicit benchmark for judging whether a company's AI program is being managed realistically — firms promising deterministic AI outcomes are either overpromising or deploying in the wrong places.
insights.quote: Build a team culture that treats a 70% success rate as a win and mines the 30% failure rate for what it teaches.

insights.claim: First AI deployments should deliberately avoid regulatory reporting and any process where a wrong answer could touch someone's safety, and instead target processes where being mostly right is useful and a human can stay in the loop.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Implies compliance and safety-critical software categories will be among the last to see AI-driven economics change, extending the runway for incumbent deterministic vendors in those niches.
insights.quote: Don’t dive into regulatory reporting or any other place where a wrong answer could touch someone’s safety.
insights.locator: Just be deliberate about where you start.

insights.claim: Leaders are told explicitly that they will not get AI decisions right and are not supposed to, reframing the executive job as moving, staying honest about what works, and retaining employee trust rather than pre-computing a correct answer.
insights.speaker: Tiger Tyagarajan
insights.so_what: Expect more public AI pivots, shutdowns and restarts from large companies — treat a killed AI project as a sign of discipline rather than automatically as a failed strategy.
insights.quote: The job isn’t to have the perfect answer before you move.
insights.locator: One last thing, since I know how lonely
